passages.title: Rooftop Beekeeping in Northbridge
passages.instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When the city of Northbridge relaxed its building rules in 2009, a handful of office owners began placing beehives on their flat roofs. The first hives were installed by a retired chemistry teacher, Mara Ellison, who persuaded the manager of a printing company to let her use the empty space above his workshop. Within three years, more than forty roofs in the old harbour district carried hives.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Supporters argue that city bees are healthier than their rural relatives. Parks, private gardens and the lime trees that line the main avenues flower at different times, so urban colonies can find nectar from early spring until late autumn. Farmland, by contrast, often offers a single crop that blooms for only a few weeks.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The honey itself has become a small local industry. Each rooftop produces a slightly different flavour depending on the nearest trees, and several cafés now sell jars labelled with the street where the honey was collected. A typical rooftop hive yields around twelve kilograms a year, although output falls sharply after a wet summer.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone welcomes the trend. Some residents worry about stings, and a few gardeners claim that so many hives compete with wild pollinators such as bumblebees. The city council has not yet published any study on this question, but it now requires new beekeepers to register their hives and to complete a short training course.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Ellison herself believes the future lies in education rather than honey. Her group runs school visits every Thursday, during which pupils wear protective veils and inspect a hive frame. 'Children who have held a frame of bees,' she says, 'never look at a flower in quite the same way again.'

passages.title: The Lantern Clock Project
passages.instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 2017 a group of volunteers in the market town of Felbury set out to rebuild a lantern clock that had stood in the town hall until a fire destroyed it in 1890. Only a single photograph and a few written descriptions survived.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first task was to work out how large the clock had been. By comparing the photograph with the window frames, which are still in place, the team calculated that the dial measured just under forty centimetres across.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Money proved harder to find than information. A local bakery agreed to donate a share of its weekend sales, and a crowdfunding page eventually raised the remaining funds in less than two months.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Engineer Dalia Okafor designed the gear train using modern software, but insisted that every wheel be cut by hand. 'A machine-cut wheel would keep better time,' she admitted, 'but it would not be the clock that Felbury lost.'

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Historian Peter Lund spent a winter in county archives searching for the name of the original maker. He found a receipt suggesting that the clock had been bought second-hand from a neighbouring village.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The finished clock was unveiled in 2021. It loses about a minute each week, and a rota of volunteers now winds it every Saturday morning, an arrangement that has become a small weekly event in the town.

passages.title: Why Do We Hum?
passages.instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most of us hum without noticing. We hum while cooking, while waiting for a bus, or while trying to remember the name of a song. Yet humming has received far less attention from researchers than singing or speech, and I believe that this neglect is a mistake.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One reason humming deserves attention is that it seems to calm the person who does it. Several small studies have reported slower breathing in volunteers who hummed for five minutes. These studies were short and involved few people, so their results should be treated with caution, but they are consistent with what many people say about their own experience.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second reason is social. Parents in almost every culture hum to babies, often before the child can understand a single word. In my view, this suggests that humming may be one of the oldest ways in which humans share feelings with one another.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Critics reply that humming is simply singing with the mouth closed and needs no separate explanation. I find this argument unconvincing. People who would never sing in public will happily hum in a shop, which implies that the two activities feel very different to the person doing them.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: None of this means that humming is a cure for stress or a secret language. It does mean that a habit we share with nearly everyone we meet deserves at least one serious, large-scale study.
